stem: You want Dependabot to group related minor and patch updates into a single pull request to reduce noise. Which configuration supports this?

options.text: A groups setting in dependabot.yml
Setting open-pull-requests-limit to zero
Enabling push protection
Adding a CODEOWNERS entry

explanationCorrect: Dependabot supports a groups key in the configuration so that multiple related updates are combined into one pull request instead of many separate ones.
explanationIncorrect: Setting open-pull-requests-limit to zero would stop Dependabot from opening update pull requests at all, not group them. Push protection is a secret scanning feature unrelated to how update pull requests are batched. A CODEOWNERS entry routes reviews and does not change how Dependabot groups updates.

stem: Dependabot alerts distinguish direct from transitive dependencies. Why does that distinction matter for remediation?

options.text: A transitive vulnerability may require updating the direct dependency that pulls it in, not the transitive package directly
Transitive dependencies cannot be vulnerable
Direct dependencies are never scanned
Transitive dependencies must be vendored to be fixed

explanationCorrect: Because a transitive dependency is pulled in by another package, fixing it often means bumping the direct dependency to a version that resolves a patched transitive one, so knowing which is which guides the fix.
explanationIncorrect: Transitive dependencies certainly can be vulnerable; that is precisely why they are tracked. Direct dependencies are scanned as well, so claiming they are never scanned is false. Vendoring is not a requirement to fix a transitive dependency; updating the chain that brings it in is the usual path.

stem: Which of these does Dependabot need to determine your dependencies for an ecosystem like npm?

options.text: The manifest and lockfile such as package.json and package-lock.json
A running instance of the application
A CODEOWNERS file
The compiled production bundle only

explanationCorrect: Dependabot reads the ecosystem's manifest and lockfile, for example package.json and package-lock.json, to know which packages and versions your project depends on.
explanationIncorrect: It performs static analysis of dependency files and does not need a running instance of the application. A CODEOWNERS file is about review routing and tells Dependabot nothing about dependencies. The compiled production bundle alone typically obscures the declared dependency versions Dependabot relies on, so the manifest and lockfile are what it uses.

stem: Which three capabilities are the core pillars of GitHub Advanced Security?

options.text: Code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review/Dependabot
Pages, Projects, and Discussions
Actions, Packages, and Codespaces
Wiki, Insights, and Releases

explanationCorrect: GHAS centers on code scanning for vulnerable code, secret scanning for leaked credentials, and supply-chain security via the dependency graph, Dependabot, and dependency review.
explanationIncorrect: Pages, Projects, and Discussions are collaboration and publishing features, not security scanning. Actions, Packages, and Codespaces are automation, artifact hosting, and development environments, not the GHAS security pillars. Wiki, Insights, and Releases are documentation, analytics, and distribution features unrelated to the security capabilities GHAS provides.

stem: For public repositories on GitHub.com, which statement about GHAS features is accurate?

options.text: Code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency features are available at no cost
GHAS features are never available on public repositories
Only paid organizations can use them on public repos
They require a self-hosted server

explanationCorrect: On public repositories these security features are offered free of charge, which is why open-source projects can use code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review without a GHAS license.
explanationIncorrect: They are available on public repositories, so the claim that they never are is wrong. They do not require a paid organization for public repos; the free availability is exactly the point. They do not require a self-hosted server; these run on GitHub.com for public repositories.

stem: In an enterprise, how is a GHAS license typically consumed?

options.text: Per active committer to repositories where GHAS features are enabled
Per repository regardless of contributors
Per workflow run
Per gigabyte of code scanned

explanationCorrect: GHAS is licensed by unique active committers on repositories with the features enabled, so the same person committing to several enabled repositories still consumes one seat.
explanationIncorrect: It is not billed simply per repository; the seat model counts committers, so one repo with many committers or many repos with one committer bill differently. It is not billed per workflow run; that is closer to Actions minute billing, a separate meter. It is not billed per gigabyte of scanned code; volume of code is not the licensing unit.

stem: Where can an organization see an aggregated view of code scanning, secret scanning, and Dependabot alerts across repositories?

options.text: The Security overview
The Insights tab
The Actions tab
The Packages page

explanationCorrect: The Security overview aggregates alerts from code scanning, secret scanning, and Dependabot across an organization's repositories, giving security teams a single place to assess posture.
explanationIncorrect: The Insights tab shows traffic and contribution analytics, not aggregated security alerts. The Actions tab lists workflow runs, not security findings. The Packages page manages published artifacts and has no security alert aggregation.

stem: Which feature lets maintainers privately collaborate on and disclose a vulnerability in their own project?

options.text: Repository security advisories with a temporary private fork
A public issue labeled security
A pinned Discussion
A protected branch

explanationCorrect: Repository security advisories provide a private space, including a temporary private fork, where maintainers can discuss, fix, and coordinate disclosure of a vulnerability before publishing.
explanationIncorrect: A public issue labeled security is visible to everyone, defeating the confidentiality needed before disclosure. A pinned Discussion is also public and not designed for coordinated vulnerability handling. A protected branch controls merges but offers no private collaboration or disclosure workflow.

stem: What is the purpose of a CodeQL analysis running on a schedule in addition to on pull requests?

options.text: To catch newly disclosed query improvements and drift on the default branch even without new PRs
To replace pull request analysis entirely
To reduce Actions minutes
To rotate secrets nightly

explanationCorrect: A scheduled scan re-analyzes the default branch periodically so that improved queries and issues not tied to a recent pull request are still surfaced, keeping the baseline current.
explanationIncorrect: It complements rather than replaces pull request analysis, which is needed to catch issues before merge. It does not reduce Actions minutes; running additional scheduled scans consumes more, not fewer. It has nothing to do with rotating secrets, which is a secret scanning concern, not a CodeQL schedule.

stem: Which feature allows security findings from external SAST tools to be centralized in the GitHub security tab?

options.text: Uploading SARIF results to code scanning
Attaching a PDF report to a release
Posting findings in Discussions
Committing a results.txt file

explanationCorrect: Code scanning accepts SARIF uploads, so results from third-party static analysis tools appear as alerts in the security tab alongside CodeQL findings.
explanationIncorrect: A PDF attached to a release is not parsed into code scanning alerts and cannot be triaged like them. Posting findings in Discussions leaves them as free-form text, not structured alerts. Committing a results.txt file does not register the findings with code scanning; the supported mechanism is SARIF upload.

stem: What does enabling GHAS on a private repository unlock that is not available without it?

options.text: Code scanning and secret scanning for that private repository
Free unlimited Actions minutes
Automatic code formatting
Unlimited storage for packages

explanationCorrect: For private repositories, code scanning and secret scanning are GHAS features, so enabling GHAS is what makes those security capabilities available there.
explanationIncorrect: GHAS does not grant free unlimited Actions minutes; compute billing is separate. It does not perform automatic code formatting, which is not a security feature. It does not provide unlimited package storage; packages are governed by their own storage and billing rules.

stem: Security overview offers enablement trends and alert metrics. How does this help a security program?

options.text: It shows which repositories have features enabled and how alerts are trending, guiding coverage and prioritization
It automatically fixes all open alerts
It replaces the need for branch protection
It compiles the application for release

explanationCorrect: By revealing enablement gaps and alert trends across repositories, Security overview helps teams decide where to turn on features and which risks to tackle first, driving measurable improvement.
explanationIncorrect: It does not automatically fix alerts; remediation still requires code or configuration changes. It does not replace branch protection, which enforces merge gates that a reporting view cannot. It does not compile the application; building for release is unrelated to a security reporting dashboard.

stem: Which statement about secret scanning coverage under GHAS is correct for private repositories?

options.text: Secret scanning for private repositories requires GHAS to be enabled
Secret scanning never works on private repositories
Secret scanning on private repositories is free without GHAS
Secret scanning requires disabling the dependency graph

explanationCorrect: On private repositories, secret scanning is part of GHAS, so it must be enabled through a GHAS license to protect those repositories.
explanationIncorrect: It does work on private repositories when GHAS is enabled, so the claim that it never works is false. It is not free without GHAS on private repositories; that free tier applies to public repositories. It has no dependence on disabling the dependency graph; the two features operate independently.

stem: When triaging a large backlog of code scanning alerts, which prioritization approach is most defensible?

options.text: Prioritize by severity and exploitability, focusing first on high-severity, reachable issues
Fix alerts in the order their files appear alphabetically
Dismiss every alert older than a week
Only fix alerts reported by external contributors

explanationCorrect: Ranking by severity and whether the vulnerable path is actually reachable directs limited effort to the issues most likely to cause real harm first.
explanationIncorrect: Alphabetical file order ignores risk entirely and would delay critical fixes behind trivial ones. Dismissing alerts merely because they are old hides risk without evaluating it. Restricting fixes to alerts from external contributors ignores where the vulnerability actually is; the source of the report does not determine its severity.

stem: To stop new vulnerabilities from being merged while allowing existing ones to be paid down over time, what is a common strategy?

options.text: Fail pull requests only on newly introduced alerts, tracking pre-existing ones separately
Block all merges until every historical alert is fixed
Disable code scanning until the backlog is clear
Delete the alerts and start fresh

explanationCorrect: Gating on new alerts introduced by a pull request prevents regressions immediately while letting the team address the legacy backlog on its own schedule, a practical balance.
explanationIncorrect: Blocking all merges until every historical alert is fixed halts delivery and is rarely feasible for a large backlog. Disabling code scanning removes the very signal you need and lets new issues slip in. Deleting alerts to start fresh throws away information about real risks without fixing anything.

stem: A dependency has a vulnerability with no fixed version yet available. What is a reasonable interim mitigation?

options.text: Apply a workaround such as input validation or feature disabling while tracking the alert until a patch lands
Dismiss the alert permanently and forget it
Downgrade to any older version regardless of its own vulnerabilities
Remove all logging so the issue is not visible

explanationCorrect: When no patch exists, applying a compensating control such as validating input or disabling the affected feature reduces exposure, and keeping the alert open ensures you upgrade once a fix is released.
explanationIncorrect: Dismissing permanently and forgetting removes the reminder to upgrade when a fix arrives, leaving you exposed. Blindly downgrading may reintroduce older, possibly worse vulnerabilities. Removing logging hides evidence rather than reducing risk and would hamper incident response, so it is never a mitigation.

stem: Why is pinning actions to a full commit SHA considered a remediation best practice for workflow supply-chain risk?

options.text: A SHA is immutable, so a compromised or re-pointed tag cannot swap in malicious code
It makes workflows run faster
It grants the workflow more permissions
It disables the need for GITHUB_TOKEN

explanationCorrect: Because a commit SHA cannot change, pinning to it guarantees the reviewed code runs even if an attacker later moves a tag to point at a malicious commit.
explanationIncorrect: Pinning has no meaningful effect on execution speed; the runner still fetches the action. It does not grant more permissions; permissions are controlled separately by the permissions block. It does not remove the need for GITHUB_TOKEN, which is still provided to the job independently of how actions are pinned.

stem: A workflow needs write access only to issues but currently runs with broad permissions. What is the recommended remediation?

options.text: Set a least-privilege permissions block granting issues: write and nothing else
Grant contents: write to be safe
Use a personal access token with full scope
Disable the workflow

explanationCorrect: Applying least privilege by scoping the permissions block to issues: write limits the blast radius if the token is misused, which is the recommended hardening for workflow tokens.
explanationIncorrect: Granting contents: write adds access the workflow does not need, widening the attack surface rather than reducing it. A full-scope personal access token is far broader than the job requires and is riskier than the scoped GITHUB_TOKEN. Disabling the workflow removes needed functionality instead of securing it, so it is not a remediation.

stem: What is the value of enabling both push protection and historical secret scanning together?

options.text: Push protection stops new leaks while historical scanning surfaces secrets already in the repository
They are redundant and one should be disabled
Together they encrypt the repository
They replace the need to rotate credentials

explanationCorrect: The two are complementary: push protection prevents secrets from entering going forward, and scanning of existing content and history finds secrets that were committed before protection was in place.
explanationIncorrect: They are not redundant; each addresses a different point in time, so disabling one leaves a gap. Enabling them does not encrypt the repository; they detect and block secrets rather than encrypt content. They do not remove the need to rotate credentials; any secret that was exposed must still be revoked and rotated.

stem: After code scanning flags SQL built from concatenated user input, what is the correct fix rather than a dismissal?

options.text: Use parameterized queries or prepared statements so input is not interpreted as SQL
Escape only single quotes and keep concatenating
Add a comment explaining the risk
Move the query into a stored procedure that still concatenates

explanationCorrect: Parameterized queries separate code from data so user input is bound as a value and cannot alter the query structure, which is the durable fix for SQL injection.
explanationIncorrect: Escaping only single quotes is incomplete and historically bypassable, so it does not reliably prevent injection. A comment documents the risk without removing it. A stored procedure that still concatenates user input into dynamic SQL remains injectable, so moving the concatenation does not fix the underlying flaw.

stem: To reduce alert fatigue without lowering security, which practice is recommended?

options.text: Tune configuration with path filters and appropriate query suites so alerts are relevant, and triage consistently
Raise the dismissal threshold so most alerts auto-close
Only scan once per quarter
Turn off notifications for the security team

explanationCorrect: Scoping analysis with path filters and choosing the right query suites keeps alerts meaningful, and consistent triage prevents a noisy backlog, addressing fatigue without hiding real issues.
explanationIncorrect: Auto-closing most alerts by raising a dismissal threshold suppresses genuine findings and lowers security. Scanning only quarterly lets vulnerabilities linger undetected between scans. Turning off the security team's notifications means real alerts go unseen, which increases risk rather than managing fatigue.

stem: Which practice best prevents secrets from being committed in the first place, complementing scanning?

options.text: Use environment variables or a secret manager and reference secrets rather than hard-coding them
Commit secrets but mark the repository private
Rename secret files to avoid detection
Store secrets in the commit message instead of files

explanationCorrect: Keeping secrets out of source by injecting them from environment variables or a secret manager means there is nothing sensitive to commit, which is the strongest preventive measure.
explanationIncorrect: Committing secrets to a private repository still stores them in history where they can leak through access or forks. Renaming files to dodge detection leaves the secret in the code and defeats the purpose of scanning. Putting secrets in commit messages simply moves them to another part of the git history that is also scanned and exposed.

stem: Why should security scanning be integrated into the pull request workflow rather than only run after merge?

options.text: Catching issues before merge is cheaper and prevents vulnerabilities from reaching the main branch
Post-merge scanning is impossible
Pull request scanning uses no compute
It removes the need to ever scan the default branch

explanationCorrect: Shifting scanning left to the pull request stage surfaces problems while they are small and unmerged, which is cheaper to fix and keeps the protected branch clean.
explanationIncorrect: Post-merge scanning is entirely possible and often still done on a schedule, so that claim is false. Pull request scanning does consume compute like any workflow. It does not remove the need to scan the default branch; scheduled scans there remain valuable for catching drift and applying improved queries.

stem: CodeQL analyzes code by first building what intermediate representation that queries then run against?

options.text: A relational database of the code extracted during a build or scan
A plain-text index of source lines
A container image of the repository
A dependency lockfile

explanationCorrect: CodeQL extracts the code into a relational database that captures the program's structure and data flow, and queries are then evaluated against that database.
explanationIncorrect: A plain-text line index cannot express the control- and data-flow relationships CodeQL queries rely on. A container image packages a runtime environment, not the queryable semantic model CodeQL needs. A lockfile lists dependency versions and is unrelated to the CodeQL database that powers analysis.

stem: For a compiled language like Java or C++, CodeQL usually needs to observe the build to create its database. Which mode lets CodeQL build the database without you supplying explicit build commands?

options.text: Autobuild, which attempts to detect and run a standard build
Manual build with no commands at all
None mode, which skips building entirely for compiled languages
Interpreted mode, forcing tracing without compilation

explanationCorrect: Autobuild inspects the repository and attempts to run a conventional build so CodeQL can trace compilation and populate the database for compiled languages.
explanationIncorrect: A manual build with no commands would leave a compiled language unbuilt, so no database is created. There is no none mode that skips building yet still analyzes a compiled language correctly. Interpreted mode is not a CodeQL build option; the mechanism for automatic building is autobuild.

stem: Code scanning results from CodeQL and third-party tools are uploaded to GitHub in which standard format?

options.text: SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format)
JUnit XML
SPDX
CycloneDX

explanationCorrect: GitHub code scanning ingests results in SARIF, a standard JSON format for static analysis findings, which lets third-party tools integrate with the Security tab.
explanationIncorrect: JUnit XML reports test results, not static analysis findings. SPDX and CycloneDX are software bill-of-materials formats describing components and licenses, not code scanning alerts, so SARIF is the correct interchange format for code scanning.

stem: You want code scanning to run on every pull request and also on a weekly schedule as a safety net. Which triggers do you put in the CodeQL workflow?

options.text: pull_request and schedule (cron)
workflow_dispatch only
release and deployment
issues and issue_comment

explanationCorrect: Triggering on pull_request scans incoming changes and a scheduled cron run provides periodic full scans as a backstop.
explanationIncorrect: workflow_dispatch alone only runs on manual invocation, missing automatic PR coverage. release and deployment fire at ship time, not on every PR or weekly. issues and issue_comment respond to issue activity and never scan code, so pull_request plus schedule is the right pairing.

stem: A CodeQL query pack you want emphasizes finding more issues at the cost of more false positives. Which query suite selects that broader set?

options.text: security-extended (and security-and-quality) beyond the default suite
The minimal suite, which is the broadest
The default suite, which always returns the most alerts
The style suite, which finds security issues

explanationCorrect: The security-extended suite runs additional queries beyond the default, surfacing more potential issues with a higher chance of false positives, and security-and-quality adds maintainability queries too.
explanationIncorrect: There is no minimal suite that is broader than extended; broader means more queries, not fewer. The default suite is tuned for precision and returns fewer alerts than extended. A style suite would target formatting or maintainability, not the broader security coverage the extended suite provides.

stem: A developer marks a code scanning alert as a false positive so it stops appearing as open. Which resolution is appropriate and audited?

options.text: Dismiss the alert with a reason such as False positive or Won't fix
Delete the source file that triggered it
Disable code scanning for the whole repository
Rename the alert's rule id

explanationCorrect: Alerts are dismissed with a documented reason like False positive or Won't fix, which records who dismissed it and why while keeping an audit trail.
explanationIncorrect: Deleting the file removes real code to silence one alert and is not a resolution workflow. Disabling code scanning repository-wide hides all alerts, not just the false positive. Renaming a rule id is not something a user does to resolve an alert, so dismissing with a reason is the correct, audited action.

stem: CodeQL taint tracking flags a vulnerability where user input reaches a dangerous sink. In taint analysis terms, what are the two ends of that flow called?

options.text: A source (untrusted input) and a sink (sensitive operation)
A root and a leaf
A producer and a consumer topic
A head and a tail commit

explanationCorrect: Taint tracking follows data from a source of untrusted input to a sink where using that data is dangerous, and a flagged path connects the two.
explanationIncorrect: Root and leaf describe tree structures, not taint endpoints. Producer and consumer topic are messaging concepts, unrelated to data-flow analysis. Head and tail commit refer to Git history, not to the input-to-sink flow CodeQL models, so source and sink is the correct terminology.

stem: Secret scanning push protection does what when a developer tries to push a commit containing a recognized secret?

options.text: Blocks the push and requires the developer to remove or explicitly bypass the secret
Silently rewrites the commit to redact the secret
Allows the push but emails the secret to admins
Rotates the credential automatically at the provider

explanationCorrect: Push protection stops the push when a supported secret pattern is detected, prompting the developer to remove it or provide a bypass reason before proceeding.
explanationIncorrect: GitHub does not silently rewrite a developer's commit contents. Emailing the secret would itself expose the credential and is not how it works. Automatic rotation at the upstream provider is beyond GitHub's control and is not part of push protection, which simply blocks the push.

stem: For certain supported secret types, GitHub can notify the credential issuer when a match is found in a public repository. What is this capability called?

options.text: Partner (secret scanning) validity and partner alerts, via the secret scanning partner program
Dependabot security updates
Code scanning autofix
Branch protection webhooks

explanationCorrect: Through the secret scanning partner program, GitHub notifies participating providers when their secret patterns are detected in public repositories so they can validate or revoke the credential.
explanationIncorrect: Dependabot security updates open PRs for vulnerable dependencies, unrelated to notifying secret issuers. Code scanning autofix suggests fixes for code alerts, not credential leaks to partners. Branch protection webhooks concern merge rules and event delivery, not the partner notification flow for leaked secrets.

stem: An organization has secrets that follow an internal custom format not covered by built-in detectors. How can they still catch these in secret scanning?

options.text: Define a custom pattern using a regular expression
File a support ticket for every commit
Rely on Dependabot to detect them
Add the secrets to a .gitignore pattern

explanationCorrect: Secret scanning supports custom patterns defined with regular expressions, letting organizations detect their own credential formats.
explanationIncorrect: Filing a ticket per commit is not a scanning mechanism and would not scale. Dependabot addresses vulnerable dependencies, not organization-specific secret formats. A .gitignore rule only prevents files from being tracked and does nothing to scan committed content, so custom regex patterns are the answer.

stem: A leaked API key was detected by secret scanning. What is the most important immediate remediation step?

options.text: Revoke or rotate the exposed credential at its provider
Only delete the commit from history and stop there
Mark the alert as a false positive
Make the repository private and consider it resolved

explanationCorrect: Because a committed secret may already have been copied, the essential step is to revoke or rotate the credential so the exposed value no longer works.
explanationIncorrect: Deleting the commit does not invalidate a secret that may already have been captured from history or forks. Marking a real leak as a false positive hides it without fixing anything. Making the repo private does not undo prior exposure, so rotating the credential is the critical action.

stem: A developer legitimately needs to commit a placeholder that matches a secret pattern and hits push protection. What is the sanctioned way to proceed?

options.text: Bypass the block by selecting a reason (for example, used in tests or false positive), which is recorded
Disable secret scanning for the organization
Force-push with --no-verify to skip server checks
Base64-encode the value so it is not detected

explanationCorrect: Push protection lets an author bypass the block by choosing a documented reason, and that bypass is recorded and can alert administrators for review.
explanationIncorrect: Disabling secret scanning org-wide removes protection for everyone to unblock one push. Server-side push protection is not skipped by a local --no-verify hook, which only affects client hooks. Encoding the value to dodge detection is exactly the evasion the control is meant to catch, so the recorded bypass reason is the sanctioned path.

stem: Where do secret scanning alerts appear for a repository so security teams can triage them?

options.text: Under the Security tab, in the Secret scanning alerts section
In the repository's Actions tab
In the Pull requests tab only
In the repository wiki

explanationCorrect: Secret scanning alerts are listed in the Security tab under their own section where teams can review and resolve them.
explanationIncorrect: The Actions tab shows workflow runs, not secret alerts. The Pull requests tab lists PRs and may show inline push-protection prompts but is not the alert triage list. The wiki holds documentation, not security alerts, so the Security tab is where secret scanning alerts live.

stem: Secret scanning historically scans the entire Git history of a repository when first enabled, not just new commits. Why does this matter?

options.text: Secrets committed long ago remain valid and exposed until rotated, so historical detection is essential
Only the latest commit can ever contain a secret
History scanning replaces the need to rotate credentials
Older commits are automatically deleted after scanning

explanationCorrect: A secret buried in old history is still a live credential until it is revoked, so scanning the full history surfaces exposures that a commits-only scan would miss.
explanationIncorrect: Secrets can appear in any commit, not only the latest, which is why full-history scanning matters. Detecting a historical secret does not rotate it; rotation is still required. GitHub does not delete older commits after scanning, so preserving and scanning history is the point.

stem: What is the difference between Dependabot alerts and Dependabot security updates?

options.text: Alerts notify you of vulnerable dependencies; security updates open pull requests to fix them
Alerts open pull requests; security updates only send email
They are two names for the exact same feature
Alerts scan code while security updates scan secrets

explanationCorrect: Dependabot alerts inform you that a dependency has a known vulnerability, while Dependabot security updates automatically raise pull requests bumping the dependency to a fixed version.
explanationIncorrect: It is the security updates, not the alerts, that open pull requests, so that pairing is reversed. They are distinct features, not the same thing. Neither one scans your first-party code or secrets; both concern dependencies, so the alert-versus-fix distinction is the correct one.

stem: You want Dependabot to keep dependencies current on a schedule regardless of known vulnerabilities. Which feature and file configure this?

options.text: Dependabot version updates, configured in dependabot.yml
Dependabot security updates, which require no configuration file
Code scanning, configured in codeql.yml
Secret scanning custom patterns

explanationCorrect: Dependabot version updates keep dependencies up to date on a defined schedule and are configured via the dependabot.yml file in the repository.
explanationIncorrect: Security updates react to vulnerabilities rather than routinely bumping all dependencies on a schedule. Code scanning analyzes source code, not dependency versions. Secret scanning custom patterns detect credentials and have nothing to do with dependency currency, so version updates via dependabot.yml is correct.

stem: Dependency review adds what capability to pull requests?

options.text: It shows dependency changes in the PR and flags newly introduced vulnerable or disallowed dependencies before merge
It rewrites the lockfile automatically
It scans the diff for hardcoded secrets
It runs the full test suite

explanationCorrect: Dependency review surfaces the dependency changes a pull request introduces and warns about newly added vulnerable or policy-violating packages so they can be caught before merging.
explanationIncorrect: It reviews changes rather than rewriting the lockfile itself. Scanning for hardcoded secrets is the job of secret scanning, not dependency review. Running tests is what CI workflows do, so dependency review's distinct value is catching risky dependency changes at the PR stage.

stem: Which feature generates the data that powers dependency graph, Dependabot alerts, and dependency review by parsing manifest and lock files?

options.text: The dependency graph
The CodeQL database
The Git object store
The Actions cache

explanationCorrect: The dependency graph parses manifests and lockfiles to enumerate dependencies, and that graph underpins Dependabot alerts and dependency review.
explanationIncorrect: The CodeQL database models source code for code scanning, not the dependency inventory. The Git object store holds commits and blobs but does not by itself compute the dependency relationships. The Actions cache speeds up workflows and has no role in dependency enumeration, so the dependency graph is the foundation.

stem: A team wants dependency review to fail the pull request check when a dependency with a high-severity vulnerability is introduced. How do they enforce this in CI?

options.text: Use the dependency-review-action and set a fail-on-severity threshold
Enable Dependabot security updates only
Add the dependency to .gitignore
Turn on secret scanning push protection

explanationCorrect: The dependency-review-action runs in a workflow and can fail the check based on a configured severity threshold, blocking merges that add high-severity vulnerabilities.
explanationIncorrect: Security updates open fix PRs after the fact and do not fail a PR that introduces a vulnerable dependency. Adding a dependency to .gitignore does not stop it from being installed and is irrelevant. Secret scanning push protection blocks credentials, not vulnerable dependencies, so the dependency-review-action with fail-on-severity is the enforcement mechanism.

stem: Dependabot alerts draw on which curated data source for known vulnerabilities affecting open-source packages?

options.text: The GitHub Advisory Database
The GitHub Marketplace
The npm audit cache exclusively
The repository's own issue tracker

explanationCorrect: Dependabot alerts are based on the GitHub Advisory Database, a curated set of vulnerabilities mapped to affected package versions.
explanationIncorrect: The Marketplace lists apps and actions, not vulnerability advisories. npm audit is one ecosystem's tool and is not the cross-ecosystem source Dependabot relies on. A repository's issue tracker holds project-specific issues, not curated CVE data, so the Advisory Database is the source.

stem: A Dependabot version-update pull request bundles too many ecosystems at once and is noisy. Which dependabot.yml concept lets you separate updates by ecosystem and directory?

options.text: Separate updates entries, each with its own package-ecosystem and directory
A single wildcard entry covering everything
Branch protection rules
A CODEOWNERS file

explanationCorrect: Each entry under updates in dependabot.yml targets a specific package-ecosystem and directory, so you can configure and schedule them independently.
explanationIncorrect: There is no single wildcard entry that spans all ecosystems; each ecosystem is configured explicitly. Branch protection governs merges, not how Dependabot groups updates. CODEOWNERS assigns reviewers by path and does not control Dependabot's per-ecosystem configuration, so separate updates entries are the mechanism.

stem: Which set of features is included under GitHub Advanced Security for a repository?

options.text: Code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review (with the security overview)
Only Dependabot version updates
Pages, Discussions, and Projects
Only branch protection rules

explanationCorrect: GHAS bundles code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review, surfaced together through the security overview.
explanationIncorrect: Dependabot version updates are available broadly and are not the defining GHAS bundle by themselves. Pages, Discussions, and Projects are collaboration features unrelated to Advanced Security. Branch protection is a general repository setting, not a GHAS feature, so the scanning-and-review bundle is what GHAS provides.

stem: On GitHub Enterprise Cloud, how is GHAS typically billed, which motivates enabling it selectively?

options.text: Per active committer (unique committers to repositories with GHAS enabled)
Per repository regardless of activity
Per workflow run minute
Per code scanning alert raised

explanationCorrect: GHAS is licensed by active committer, counting unique committers to repositories that have GHAS enabled, which is why organizations enable it where it matters.
explanationIncorrect: It is not a flat per-repository charge independent of who commits. It is not metered by workflow minutes, which is how Actions usage is billed. It is not charged per alert, since findings themselves are not the billing unit, so the active-committer model is correct.

stem: The security overview dashboard at the organization level primarily helps security teams do what?

options.text: See aggregated alert status across repositories to prioritize remediation
Edit source code directly across all repos
Manage billing invoices
Configure Pages sites

explanationCorrect: The security overview aggregates code, secret, and dependency alert status across an organization's repositories so teams can spot risk and prioritize fixes.
explanationIncorrect: It is a reporting and triage surface, not a code editor for bulk changes. Billing invoices are handled in billing settings, not the security overview. Configuring Pages is a publishing concern unrelated to the security dashboard, so cross-repo alert visibility is its purpose.

stem: Which GHAS feature is available at no cost on public repositories?

options.text: Code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review are free on public repositories
None; GHAS always requires a license even on public repos
Only secret scanning, and only after purchase
Only dependency review, on private repos only

explanationCorrect: On public repositories, code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review are available at no charge, whereas private repositories require GHAS licensing.
explanationIncorrect: It is not true that a license is always required, since public repos get these features free. Limiting it to only paid secret scanning ignores the free public-repo coverage. Restricting dependency review to private repos is backwards, as the free tier is on public repositories.

stem: An organization wants GHAS automatically turned on for every new repository created. Which setting accomplishes this?

options.text: Enable GHAS features by default for new repositories in organization security settings
Add a workflow that runs on repository creation
Put a dependabot.yml in a template branch
Require signed commits organization-wide

explanationCorrect: Organization security settings include options to enable GHAS features by default for newly created repositories, applying the policy automatically.
explanationIncorrect: There is no repository-creation workflow trigger that toggles GHAS licensing. A dependabot.yml only configures Dependabot, not the full GHAS feature set. Requiring signed commits is a separate integrity control and does not enable scanning features, so the default-on organization setting is correct.

stem: Security teams can automate reactions to GHAS alerts by consuming which programmatic surfaces?

options.text: The REST/GraphQL APIs and webhooks for code scanning, secret scanning, and Dependabot alerts
Only the web UI, since alerts have no API
The Git protocol packfiles
The Pages build logs

explanationCorrect: GHAS alerts are exposed through REST and GraphQL APIs and webhook events, letting teams build automation and integrations around them.
explanationIncorrect: Alerts are not UI-only; there are documented APIs. Git packfiles carry repository objects, not alert data. Pages build logs concern site publishing and contain no alert information, so the alert APIs and webhooks are the integration surfaces.

stem: Which statement best distinguishes secret scanning from code scanning?

options.text: Secret scanning looks for exposed credentials in content; code scanning analyzes code for vulnerabilities and errors
Both only analyze dependency manifests
Secret scanning compiles code while code scanning reads text
They are the same feature under two names

explanationCorrect: Secret scanning searches repository content for leaked credentials by pattern, while code scanning statically analyzes source code to find security vulnerabilities and coding errors.
explanationIncorrect: Neither is limited to dependency manifests; that is the dependency graph's domain. Secret scanning does not compile code, and describing the pair that way misstates both. They are separate features with different goals, so the credentials-versus-code-analysis distinction is correct.

stem: To reduce noise and drive fixes, what is a recommended practice for integrating code scanning into the development lifecycle?

options.text: Run scans on pull requests and require the check so issues are caught before merge
Only scan once per year during an audit
Disable PR scanning to keep pipelines fast
Review alerts only after release

explanationCorrect: Scanning on pull requests and making the result a required check shifts detection left, so vulnerabilities are addressed before they merge into the default branch.
explanationIncorrect: An annual scan lets issues accumulate and reach production undetected. Disabling PR scanning removes the earliest and cheapest chance to fix problems. Reviewing alerts only after release means shipping known issues first, so PR-time required checks are the recommended practice.

stem: A large legacy codebase produces thousands of pre-existing code scanning alerts. What is a pragmatic way to prevent new issues while working down the backlog?

options.text: Focus the PR check on alerts introduced by the change while triaging the historical backlog separately
Dismiss every existing alert as a false positive
Turn off code scanning until the backlog is zero
Delete the legacy code without review

explanationCorrect: Gating pull requests on newly introduced alerts stops the backlog from growing while the historical alerts are triaged and remediated on their own track.
explanationIncorrect: Blanket-dismissing all existing alerts as false positives hides real vulnerabilities. Turning off scanning removes visibility entirely and lets new issues slip in. Deleting legacy code without review risks breaking functionality and is not a remediation strategy, so gating on new alerts is the pragmatic approach.

stem: After secret scanning finds a valid credential in history, what remediation order is correct?

options.text: Revoke or rotate the secret first, then remove it from code and history and prevent recurrence
Remove it from history first and skip rotation
Only close the alert without any other action
Rotate it only if the repo is public

explanationCorrect: Rotation comes first because the exposed value may already be compromised; then you scrub it from code and history and add push protection or patterns to prevent recurrence.
explanationIncorrect: Scrubbing history first while skipping rotation leaves a live credential usable. Closing the alert alone fixes nothing. Limiting rotation to public repos ignores that private repos leak through forks, clones, and insiders, so rotate-then-remove-then-prevent is the correct order.

stem: Which practice most reduces the risk of leaking secrets into a repository in the first place?

options.text: Enable push protection and store secrets in a secrets manager or Actions secrets, not in code
Commit secrets but add them to .gitignore afterward
Base64-encode secrets before committing
Rely solely on private repository visibility

explanationCorrect: Combining push protection with an external secrets manager or Actions secrets keeps credentials out of the codebase and blocks accidental commits at push time.
explanationIncorrect: Committing a secret then adding a .gitignore rule does not remove it from history and still exposes it. Base64 is trivially reversible and does not protect anything. Private visibility alone does not stop leaks via forks or insiders, so push protection plus a secrets manager is the strongest prevention.

stem: To keep Dependabot pull requests from overwhelming maintainers while still remediating vulnerabilities promptly, which practice helps most?

options.text: Group related updates and prioritize security updates, with CI validating each PR automatically
Disable Dependabot and update manually once a year
Auto-merge every Dependabot PR without any checks
Ignore all patch-level updates permanently

explanationCorrect: Grouping updates and prioritizing security fixes, backed by CI that validates each PR, keeps the volume manageable while ensuring vulnerabilities are addressed quickly.
explanationIncorrect: Disabling Dependabot for yearly manual updates leaves vulnerabilities open for long stretches. Auto-merging without checks risks shipping breaking or malicious updates. Permanently ignoring patch updates skips important security fixes, so grouping plus prioritized, CI-validated updates is the best practice.

stem: A CodeQL alert reports SQL injection where user input is concatenated into a query. What is the recommended fix?

options.text: Use parameterized queries or prepared statements so input is never concatenated into SQL
Dismiss the alert as a false positive
Escape the input by uppercasing it
Move the query into a stored procedure that still concatenates input

explanationCorrect: Parameterized queries or prepared statements separate code from data so untrusted input cannot alter the query structure, which is the correct remediation for SQL injection.
explanationIncorrect: Dismissing a genuine injection finding leaves the vulnerability in place. Uppercasing input does nothing to neutralize SQL metacharacters. A stored procedure that still concatenates untrusted input remains injectable, so parameterization is the real fix.

stem: To ensure security alerts get owner attention and are not merged past, which repository control complements GHAS scanning?

options.text: Required status checks and required reviews via branch protection or rulesets
Disabling the Security tab
Allowing force-pushes to the default branch
Removing CODEOWNERS

explanationCorrect: Requiring the scanning status checks to pass and requiring reviews through branch protection or rulesets ensures alerts block merges and get owner attention.
explanationIncorrect: Disabling the Security tab hides the very alerts you want to act on. Allowing force-pushes weakens branch integrity rather than enforcing review. Removing CODEOWNERS reduces required-reviewer coverage, so required checks and reviews are the controls that complement scanning.

stem: Which three capabilities are the core pillars of GitHub Advanced Security?

options.text: Code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review
Pages, Packages, and Projects
Actions, Codespaces, and Copilot
Issues, Discussions, and Wikis

explanationCorrect: GHAS centers on code scanning for vulnerabilities, secret scanning for leaked credentials, and dependency review for risky dependency changes.
explanationIncorrect: Pages, Packages, and Projects are general platform features unrelated to the security suite. Actions, Codespaces, and Copilot are productivity and CI tools, not the GHAS pillars. Issues, Discussions, and Wikis are collaboration features, so code scanning, secret scanning, and dependency review are the correct trio.

stem: Where do code scanning and secret scanning alerts appear for a repository?

options.text: Under the repository's Security tab
In the repository's Wiki
In the Projects board only
In the repository's Releases page

explanationCorrect: GHAS surfaces code scanning and secret scanning alerts in the repository's Security tab, which centralizes security findings.
explanationIncorrect: The Wiki holds documentation, not alerts. A Projects board tracks work items, not security findings. The Releases page lists shipped versions, so the Security tab is where these alerts appear.

stem: For GitHub Enterprise Cloud, which licensing basis has traditionally governed GitHub Advanced Security consumption?

options.text: A committer-based model counting unique active committers to repositories with GHAS enabled
A per-open-issue model
A per-workflow-run model
A per-star model

explanationCorrect: GHAS licensing has traditionally been measured by unique active committers to repositories where Advanced Security is enabled, so each such committer consumes a seat.
explanationIncorrect: Open issue counts have no bearing on GHAS licensing. Workflow runs relate to Actions minutes, not GHAS seats. Repository stars are a popularity metric with no licensing role, so the committer-based model is the correct basis.

stem: Which GHAS feature is available on public repositories at no cost?

options.text: Code scanning and secret scanning are free for public repositories
GHAS features are never available on public repositories
Only paid private repositories can use any scanning
Scanning requires a self-hosted server for public repos

explanationCorrect: GitHub offers code scanning and secret scanning for public repositories at no charge, making these protections broadly available to open source.
explanationIncorrect: It is false that GHAS features are never on public repos, since public repos get scanning free. Scanning is not limited to paid private repos. Public repository scanning does not require a self-hosted server, so free availability on public repos is correct.

stem: A security manager wants an organization-wide view of alerts across all repositories. Which GHAS capability provides this?

options.text: The security overview dashboard at the organization level
A single repository's Insights tab
The Actions tab
The repository's commit history

explanationCorrect: The security overview aggregates code scanning, secret scanning, and Dependabot alerts across an organization's repositories in one dashboard.
explanationIncorrect: A single repository's Insights tab shows metrics for that repo only, not an org-wide roll-up. The Actions tab shows workflow runs, not security alerts. Commit history lists changes, not aggregated alerts, so the organization security overview is the right capability.

stem: Which statement best describes how GHAS integrates results into the pull request workflow?

options.text: Findings can appear as PR checks and inline annotations so issues are caught before merge
Findings are only emailed weekly
Findings are hidden until after deployment
Findings appear only in the wiki

explanationCorrect: GHAS surfaces code scanning and dependency review results directly on pull requests as checks and inline annotations, shifting detection left before merge.
explanationIncorrect: GHAS does not restrict findings to a weekly email; results are near-real-time on PRs. It does not hide findings until after deployment, which would defeat shift-left goals. Findings are not confined to the wiki, so PR checks and inline annotations describe the integration correctly.

stem: Which format do code scanning tools use to upload results to GitHub so they appear as alerts?

options.text: SARIF
CSV
PNG
INI

explanationCorrect: Code scanning consumes SARIF, the Static Analysis Results Interchange Format, so any tool that emits SARIF can upload findings as alerts.
explanationIncorrect: CSV is a generic tabular format that code scanning does not ingest as alerts. PNG is an image format, not analysis results. INI is a configuration format, so SARIF is the correct interchange format for code scanning results.

stem: Which GHAS feature specifically warns you about vulnerable or malicious dependencies introduced in a pull request?

options.text: Dependency review
Secret scanning
Code scanning of first-party code
Branch protection

explanationCorrect: Dependency review inspects the dependency changes in a pull request and flags additions of known-vulnerable packages before they merge.
explanationIncorrect: Secret scanning looks for leaked credentials, not dependency risk. Code scanning of first-party code analyzes your own source, not third-party dependency changes. Branch protection enforces merge rules but does not analyze dependencies, so dependency review is the correct feature.

stem: An admin wants to turn on GHAS features for all new repositories in an organization automatically. Where is this default set?

options.text: In the organization's code security and analysis settings, enabling features for new repositories
In each repository's README
In the runner configuration
In a workflow's concurrency block

explanationCorrect: Organization code security and analysis settings include toggles to automatically enable GHAS features for newly created repositories.
explanationIncorrect: A README is documentation and cannot enable features. Runner configuration governs job execution machines, not security defaults. A concurrency block serializes runs, so the organization code security and analysis settings are where this default lives.

stem: Which statement about secret scanning push protection is accurate?

options.text: It can block a push that contains a detected secret before it reaches the repository
It only scans after a release is published
It deletes the repository on detection
It rewrites the secret to a random value silently

explanationCorrect: Push protection intercepts a push containing a recognized secret pattern and blocks it, prompting the developer to remove the secret before it lands.
explanationIncorrect: Push protection acts at push time, not only after a release. It never deletes the repository, which would be destructive and unnecessary. It does not silently rewrite secrets, since the developer must resolve the finding, so blocking the push is the accurate behavior.

stem: When secret scanning detects a leaked token from a supported provider, what mechanism can notify that provider automatically?

options.text: Partner secret scanning, where GitHub alerts the token's issuer to validate or revoke it
A pull request comment to the provider
A wiki page update
A new release tag

explanationCorrect: Through the partner program, GitHub forwards matches for supported providers' token types to the issuer so they can validate and revoke the exposed credential.
explanationIncorrect: A PR comment notifies repository collaborators, not the external token issuer. A wiki page update is documentation and triggers no provider action. A release tag marks a version and does not contact a provider, so partner secret scanning is the correct mechanism.

stem: You want to detect leaks of your own internally issued token format. What should you configure?

options.text: A custom secret scanning pattern using a regular expression
A new branch protection rule
A CodeQL query pack
A Dependabot config

explanationCorrect: Custom patterns let you define a regular expression that matches your organization's proprietary token format so secret scanning can detect it.
explanationIncorrect: Branch protection governs merges, not secret detection. CodeQL analyzes code for vulnerabilities and is not the tool for defining secret patterns. Dependabot manages dependencies, so a custom secret scanning pattern is the right configuration.

stem: A developer needs to commit a legitimate example value that matches a secret pattern but is not a real credential. In push protection, what is the appropriate path?

options.text: Bypass the block with a documented reason such as false positive or test data, which is recorded
Disable secret scanning for the whole organization
Delete the branch
Rename the file to hide it

explanationCorrect: Push protection lets an authorized user bypass the block by selecting a reason like false positive or used in tests, and the bypass is logged for audit.
explanationIncorrect: Disabling secret scanning org-wide removes protection everywhere to solve one benign case, which is disproportionate. Deleting the branch discards the work rather than committing the example. Renaming the file does not change the matched content, so a documented, recorded bypass is the appropriate path.

stem: After a real secret is confirmed leaked and detected, what is the most important remediation step?

options.text: Revoke and rotate the exposed credential immediately
Only close the alert without other action
Add the secret to the README so it is documented
Wait for the next release to address it

explanationCorrect: Because a leaked secret may already be compromised, the priority is to revoke it and issue a new credential so the exposed one is useless.
explanationIncorrect: Closing the alert without rotating leaves the compromised secret valid. Adding it to the README exposes it further. Waiting for the next release leaves a live credential exposed in the meantime, so immediate revocation and rotation is the key step.

stem: Why is removing a secret only from the latest commit often insufficient?

options.text: The secret still exists in git history and can be recovered from earlier commits
The secret is automatically re-added by GitHub
Latest-commit removal corrupts the repository
GitHub blocks all future pushes

explanationCorrect: Git retains full history, so a secret introduced in an earlier commit remains retrievable even after the newest commit no longer contains it, which is why rotation matters most.
explanationIncorrect: GitHub does not re-add removed secrets. Removing content from the latest commit does not corrupt the repository. GitHub does not block all future pushes because of a prior secret, so the persistence in git history is the real reason.

stem: An organization wants secret scanning alerts to be triaged consistently. Which built-in state helps mark an alert that is a real but accepted risk versus a false detection?

options.text: Resolving the alert with a reason such as revoked, false positive, or used in tests
Converting the alert into a milestone
Pinning the alert to the profile
Merging the alert into main

explanationCorrect: Secret scanning alerts can be resolved with a specific reason like revoked, false positive, or used in tests, giving consistent triage semantics.
explanationIncorrect: Milestones group issues and pull requests, not security alert states. Pinning to a profile is for showcasing repositories, not triage. Alerts are not merged into a branch, so resolving with a reason is the correct triage mechanism.

stem: Which of the following best reduces the chance of committing secrets in the first place?

options.text: Enabling push protection and using environment variables or a secrets manager instead of hardcoding
Committing secrets to a private repo only
Storing secrets in code comments
Disabling all scanning

explanationCorrect: Push protection stops secrets at commit time, and sourcing credentials from environment variables or a secrets manager avoids putting them in code at all.
explanationIncorrect: A private repo still stores the secret in history and can be cloned or leaked. Code comments are still committed content and offer no protection. Disabling scanning removes the safety net entirely, so push protection plus externalized secrets is the best prevention.

stem: Secret scanning validity checks add what useful information to certain provider alerts?

options.text: Whether the detected credential is currently active or already inactive
The commit author's home address
The number of stars on the repo
The size of the repository in bytes

explanationCorrect: Validity checks query supported providers to indicate whether a detected token is still active, helping prioritize the most dangerous live leaks.
explanationIncorrect: Secret scanning does not expose an author's home address, which it has no access to. Star counts are a popularity metric unrelated to credential validity. Repository size in bytes is irrelevant to a secret's status, so active-or-inactive validity is the useful added information.

stem: Push protection is enabled but a developer's secret pattern is not covered by any default or custom pattern. What is the realistic outcome?

options.text: The secret can be pushed because push protection only blocks patterns it recognizes
The push is always blocked regardless of pattern
The repository is locked permanently
GitHub invents a pattern automatically for it

explanationCorrect: Push protection can only block secrets that match a known default or configured custom pattern, so an unrecognized format may pass, underscoring the value of custom patterns.
explanationIncorrect: It is not true that all pushes are blocked, since protection is pattern-driven. The repository is not locked permanently by a push. GitHub does not automatically invent a matching pattern for unknown formats, so an unrecognized secret can slip through.

stem: Which scope of scanning does secret scanning perform on an enabled repository by default?

options.text: It scans the full git history and new commits for known secret patterns
It scans only the repository description
It scans only open issues
It scans only the default branch's latest file listing without history

explanationCorrect: When enabled, secret scanning examines the entire git history as well as incoming commits, so previously committed secrets are also surfaced.
explanationIncorrect: It does not limit itself to the repository description. It is not restricted to open issues. It does not ignore history and look only at the current file listing, since historical leaks matter, so full-history plus new-commit scanning is correct.
